prohibited_recommendations: Do not anchor on alcohol intoxication when focal neurologic signs (ophthalmoparesis, dysarthria, ataxia, bilateral Babinski signs) persist or worsen; pursue immediate stroke imaging.
Do not delay non-contrast CT and CTA to let the patient sober up.
Do not treat the 14:00 deterioration as a new onset for IV thrombolysis: she never returned to baseline, so last known well remains the previous evening.
Do not give glucose-containing fluids before thiamine in this patient with alcohol use disorder.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (23:00 the previous evening, when she went to bed; she improved by 10:30 but never returned to baseline, so the 14:00 deterioration does not reset it) and the NIHSS (14).

IV thrombolysis: do not give, because last known well (23:00) is 15 hours before the deterioration and she never returned to baseline. The extended-window criteria do not apply either: she is a thrombectomy candidate, and the decision falls about 11 hours after the midpoint of sleep (about 03:00). Thrombectomy: proceed for the basilar artery occlusion; do not wait for any further study.

Proceed to mechanical thrombectomy for the basilar artery occlusion (NIHSS 14, pre-stroke mRS 0, PC-ASPECTS 6, within 24 hours of last known well; AHA/ASA 2026 §4.7.3, COR 1); keep blood pressure at or below 185/110 mmHg before the procedure and do not target systolic below 140 mmHg after successful recanalization.

Give high-dose IV thiamine (for example 200 to 500 mg three times daily) before any further glucose-containing fluid: she has alcohol use disorder with ophthalmoparesis, ataxia and altered consciousness, and Wernicke encephalopathy can coexist with the brainstem infarct.
Keep nil by mouth until a formal swallowing assessment (dysphagia, reduced gag) and watch airway protection (GCS 13, somnolent).

Admit to a stroke unit or neurocritical care with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours and frequent neurological checks for cerebellar swelling (bilateral cerebellar infarcts, fourth ventricle effaced), with early neurosurgical involvement for ventriculostomy or suboccipital decompression if hydrocephalus or brainstem compression develops.
Monitor for alcohol withdrawal with a validated scale (CIWA-Ar) and treat it symptom-triggered; replace potassium (3.4 mEq/L) and magnesium (1.6 mg/dL).

Classify the mechanism as undetermined: the PFO is probably incidental (RoPE score 4: hypertension, smoking, age 50, no cortical infarct) and 48-hour monitoring found no atrial fibrillation; arrange prolonged ambulatory rhythm monitoring (30-day event monitor or implantable loop recorder) after discharge.

Start antiplatelet therapy once post-thrombectomy imaging at 24 hours excludes haemorrhage; high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg, LDL 138 mg/dL, target below 70 mg/dL); long-term blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg; smoking and alcohol cessation support.

Last known well is 23:00 the previous evening. She improved by 10:30 but never returned to baseline (still unable to walk, nystagmus persisting), so the 14:00 deterioration is progression rather than a new onset, and IV thrombolysis is outside the 4.5-hour window.

CTA shows a complete mid-to-distal basilar occlusion. NIHSS 14, pre-stroke mRS 0 and PC-ASPECTS 6 (both cerebellar hemispheres and the pons) meet the criteria for thrombectomy within 24 hours of last known well (AHA/ASA 2026 §4.7.3, COR 1; ATTENTION and BAOCHE, NEJM 2022).
NIHSS 14: LOC 1, questions 2, commands 1, gaze 1 (bilateral sixth nerve palsies), face 1, each arm 1, each leg 1, limb ataxia 2, dysarthria 2. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6).

Ophthalmoparesis, ataxia and altered consciousness in alcohol use disorder: the dorsal pontine infarct explains them, but Wernicke encephalopathy can coexist and is prevented by thiamine before glucose.
Bilateral cerebellar infarcts with fourth ventricular effacement need monitoring for swelling and obstructive hydrocephalus.

The PFO (moderate shunt on Valsalva) is probably incidental: RoPE score 4 (hypertension, smoking, age 50, no cortical infarct). With no atrial fibrillation in 48 hours and no vertebrobasilar atheroma or dissection, the mechanism remains undetermined pending prolonged rhythm monitoring.

clinical_pearls: Posterior circulation strokes are missed more frequently than anterior circulation strokes because their symptoms (vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria) overlap with common benign conditions and intoxication
DWI sensitivity for posterior circulation stroke in the first 24 hours is only 72-80%, compared to >95% for anterior circulation stroke
The 'stuttering' or fluctuating course in basilar artery occlusion results from intermittent collateral compensation and should trigger immediate vascular imaging
Approximately 25% of the general population has a PFO; its significance increases dramatically when combined with venous thrombosis history and thrombophilia
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle. The initial presentation mimics alcohol intoxication with a high ethanol level, the course fluctuates, and the 14:00 deterioration tempts a new-onset thrombolysis decision although she never returned to baseline. The critical findings are the persistent focal brainstem signs and the basilar artery occlusion on CTA, which leads to late-window thrombectomy (ATTENTION, BAOCHE). Alcohol-related laboratory abnormalities, a remote DVT and a PFO are red herrings or secondary issues.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Katarina Novak is a 50-year-old right-handed woman brought to the emergency department at approximately 07:00 by her husband, who reports he was unable to awaken her that morning. She had gone to bed at about 23:00 the previous evening after drinking approximately one bottle of wine, and he had noticed nothing unusual apart from the drinking at that time. She is fully independent and works full time. On initial evaluation, the patient was somnolent with moderate dysarthria, horizontal gaze-directed nystagmus, marked truncal ataxia, and bilateral upper and lower extremity incoordination. Given her known history of episodic heavy alcohol use, the clinical team initially attributed her symptoms to acute alcohol intoxication. Serum ethanol level returned at 2.3 per mille, consistent with significant intoxication. Intravenous fluids were started and she was placed on hourly neurological observation. By approximately 10:30, her clinical status appeared to improve substantially: she became more alert, her dysarthria resolved, and her ataxia improved significantly, although she still could not walk without help and the nystagmus persisted. However, at approximately 14:00, the nursing staff documented acute deterioration with rapidly worsening somnolence, new complaints of diplopia, difficulty swallowing, and recurrence of severe horizontal nystagmus and dysarthria. The patient's husband, who had remained at bedside, confirmed she had been conversant and sitting up comfortably just 30 minutes prior. There was no witnessed seizure activity, no head trauma, and no febrile illness. She had not vomited and there was no headache reported during her lucid interval. She was urgently re-evaluated.
